blocks.heading: Why the length matters
text: A model composition is only useful if the pupil reading it believes they could write something like it. A beautiful piece of 400 words handed to a child who must produce 100 does not raise the standard - it teaches them that good writing is something other people do.

So these grow with the grade: about a hundred words at Grade 6 and ten more for each year after it, a larger step to a hundred and sixty-five at Grade 11 where the O/L work is judged, and two hundred and fifty across both Advanced Level years, which is the length a General English answer runs to. blocks.heading: Using a model without copying it
text: The commonest mistake with model compositions is to read one and then set the same title. The class writes a slightly worse version of what they have just read, and nobody learns anything.
bullets: **Take one technique, not the whole piece.** The last line, the dialogue, the way the first sentence puts you in a place.
**Change the title before they write.** If the model is about a rainy day, set a hot day, or a day the electricity failed.
**Let them see the word count.** Knowing the target is a hundred words stops a weak writer producing four sentences and a strong one producing two pages.
**Read one aloud a week,** not ten in a lesson. A composition heard is remembered; a booklet handed out is filed.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred words each, written at the level of a Grade 6 learner of English rather than at the level of a teacher. The sentences are short, the tenses are the past simple and the present simple, and the words are ones a pupil already knows.
Each one is followed by a line saying what it shows. Read that line with the class: a model that is only admired teaches nothing, but a model a pupil can copy one trick from teaches a great deal.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 100 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 6 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 94 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. A Rainy Day
text: It rained all morning on Sunday. The sky was grey and the road outside our house was full of water.
I could not go out to play. I sat near the window and watched the rain. A small bird sat on the wall. It was wet and it looked cold.
My mother made hot tea and we drank it together. She told me a story about her school days.
In the evening the rain stopped. The trees were clean and green. A rainbow came in the sky.
I ran outside and jumped in the water. It was the best part of the day.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: One day, told in order, with the weather doing the work. Notice the last line: the writer does not say "I was happy", they show it.

blocks.heading: 2. My Pet
text: We have a dog at home. His name is Kalu because he is black.
Kalu is three years old. He is not very big but he barks loudly at strangers. When I come home from school he runs to the gate and jumps on me.
Every evening I give him rice and fish. He eats very fast. After that we play in the garden with an old ball.
Kalu sleeps near my bed at night. Sometimes he dreams and his legs move.
My father says a dog is a good friend. I think my father is right.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Simple present for what usually happens. The small detail about his legs moving in a dream is what makes the dog real.

blocks.heading: 3. My Best Friend
text: My best friend is Nimali. She sits next to me in class.
Nimali is tall and she has long hair. She is good at mathematics and she helps me when I cannot do a sum. I am better at English, so I help her with spelling.
At interval we eat together under the mango tree. She always gives me half of her biscuit.
Last month I was ill for four days. Nimali brought my books to my house and told me what the teacher taught.
A good friend is someone who does not forget you.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A person described by what they do, not by a list of adjectives. The last sentence says what the story was about.

blocks.heading: 4. Helping My Mother
text: On Saturday my mother cleans the house. Last Saturday I helped her.
First I swept the floor. Then I washed the plates and put them on the rack. My little brother tried to help but he dropped a cup. It did not break.
After that we went to the shop and bought vegetables. The bag was heavy so we carried it together.
In the afternoon my mother cooked rice and dhal. We were both tired.
She said thank you to me. I felt very proud.
Now I help her every Saturday.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Time words - first, then, after that, in the afternoon - holding the order together. The last line shows the change.

blocks.heading: 5. Our School Garden
text: Behind our classroom there is a small garden. Our class made it last year.
We planted tomatoes, chillies and some flowers. Every morning two pupils water the plants. This week it is my turn.
At first the plants were very small. Now the tomato plants are taller than my brother.
Last week we picked the first tomatoes. Our teacher counted them. There were fourteen.
We gave them to the school cook and she put them in our lunch.
It was only a small lunch but everybody said it tasted good.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Numbers and time make a story true. "Fourteen" is better than "many", and the last line is quietly funny.

blocks.heading: 6. A Bus Journey
text: Last month we went to Kandy by bus. We left our house at five in the morning.
The bus was very full. I sat near the window and my mother stood for one hour. Then a kind man gave her his seat.
Outside I saw paddy fields, small shops and a river. A woman sold vadai at the bus stop and my father bought four.
The road went up the hill and my ears felt strange.
We reached Kandy at nine o'clock. I was tired but I was happy to see the lake.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A journey is easy to write because it already has an order. Notice the ears - one small true detail is worth three sentences of description.

blocks.heading: 7. My Birthday
text: My birthday is on the tenth of June. This year I was twelve.
In the morning my mother made milk rice. I wore my new blue shirt and went to school.
At interval my friends sang for me and I gave them toffees. My teacher wrote a note in my book.
In the evening my aunt and my cousins came to our house. We ate cake and we played cricket in the garden until it was dark.
I did not get a big present. But it was a very good day.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The last two sentences together. Saying what did not happen, then saying it did not matter, is a real writer's move.

blocks.heading: 8. The New Student
text: A new boy came to our class last term. His name is Sahan.
On the first day he sat alone. He did not talk to anybody. At interval he stood near the wall and looked at the ground.
I remembered my first day at this school. I was afraid too.
So I went to him and asked his name. He told me. Then I asked him to play cricket with us.
Sahan is a very good bowler. Now he has many friends.
It took me one minute to ask his name.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The writer remembers their own first day, and that is why they act. The short last line carries the whole point.

blocks.heading: 9. The Lost Book
text: Last Tuesday I could not find my English book. I looked in my bag three times.
I was afraid because my teacher does not like carelessness.
I looked under my desk and in the cupboard. My friends helped me. We even went to the next class and asked. We could not find it anywhere.
Then a girl from Grade 7 came to our class. She had my book in her hand. She found it on the bus and she saw my name inside.
I said thank you many times.
Now I write my name in every book.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A small problem, solved by somebody else's kindness. The last line is what the writer learned, in six words.

blocks.heading: 10. Our Village Shop
text: There is a small shop at the end of our lane. Mr Piyasena keeps it.
The shop is not big. It sells bread, sugar, tea, soap and sweets. There is one old fridge near the door.
Every evening people come to buy things and to talk. They talk about the rain and the price of rice.
Mr Piyasena knows everybody's name. He knows what my mother buys on Sunday.
Sometimes he gives a toffee to a small child for nothing.
It is a small shop but our lane needs it.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A place described through the people in it. The toffee sentence tells you what kind of man he is without using one adjective.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Read one aloud, then ask what happened.** If the class can retell it in three sentences, the writing is clear. That is the standard, not long words.
**Point at one thing to copy.** The last line, or the dialogue, or the way the first sentence puts you in the place. One thing, not the whole piece.
**Give them the same title and a hundred words.** A word limit helps a weak writer more than it restricts a strong one: it stops the story wandering.
**Do not correct every mistake.** Mark the two that matter most in that piece. A page returned in red ink teaches a child that writing is dangerous.
**Read the best two aloud next lesson,** without names if the writer would rather. Pupils write for an audience, and the class is the only audience they have.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred and ten words, one step beyond Grade 6. The sentences begin to join with *but* and *because*, a line of speech appears here and there, and each piece turns once - something changes between the beginning and the end.
The English stays inside what a Grade 7 second-language learner already has. Nothing here needs a dictionary.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 110 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 7 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 110 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. The New Year
text: In April we celebrate the Sinhala and Tamil New Year. It is my favourite time of the year.
My mother starts cooking two days before. She makes kavum, kokis and milk rice. Our whole house smells sweet.
On the day we wear new clothes. My grandmother lights the hearth at the right time and we eat together.
After lunch the games begin in our lane. There is a pillow fight on a pole and a race with a spoon. Last year I won the running race for my age group.
In the evening we visit our relatives. Everybody gives something small to the children.
The best part is not the sweets. It is that everybody is at home on the same day.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A festival told through one family, not as a list of customs. The last two sentences say what it really means.

blocks.heading: 2. My Village
text: I live in a small village near Kurunegala. About sixty families live here.
There is one road through the village. On both sides there are paddy fields, and beyond the fields there is a low hill.
We have a temple, a school and three small shops. The bus comes six times a day. If you miss the last one at six o'clock you must walk.
Everybody knows everybody. When somebody is ill, three neighbours come to help before the doctor does.
In the city there is more to do. But in my village, if I shout from our gate, four people will answer.
That is why I like it here.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A place described with numbers - sixty families, six buses, three shops. Numbers make a description believable.

blocks.heading: 3. A Day at the Beach
text: Last August my uncle took us to Negombo. It was my first time at the sea.
The water was warmer than I expected. My cousin ran straight in but I walked slowly because I was afraid.
A wave came and knocked me down. I swallowed some water and it tasted terrible. Everybody laughed, and after a moment I laughed too.
We built a small house with sand. The sea washed it away twice, so we built it further back.
In the evening we ate rice packets on the sand and watched the fishing boats go out.
My hair was full of salt for two days. I did not mind.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The writer admits being afraid, then being knocked down. Small honest moments are more interesting than perfect days.

blocks.heading: 4. The Cricket Match
text: Our class played Grade 7B last Friday. We had practised for two weeks.
They batted first and made forty-two runs. We thought it would be easy.
Then we lost three wickets in the first two overs. Nobody talked after that.
I went to bat at number seven. My hands were wet. I hit two runs, then four, then I was bowled.
In the end we made thirty-nine. We lost by three runs.
Our captain said, "We lost, but we did not give up."
It is true. But three runs is a very small number, and I still think about my last ball.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The writer does not pretend to feel better than they do. The honest last sentence is what makes it real.

blocks.heading: 5. My Favourite Teacher
text: My favourite teacher is Mrs Fernando. She teaches us English.
She is not the kindest teacher in our school and she is not the strictest. She is somewhere in the middle.
When a pupil gives a wrong answer she does not say "wrong". She says, "Tell me why you thought that." Then the pupil explains, and very often finds the mistake without help.
Last term I was afraid to speak English in class. She asked me a question every single day, always an easy one, until I forgot to be afraid.
I never told her that I noticed what she was doing.
I think she knows.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: One teaching habit, shown in her actual words. "Tell me why you thought that" is worth more than ten adjectives.

blocks.heading: 6. The Power Cut
text: The electricity went off at seven o'clock, just when I opened my book.
My father found the candles and my mother found the matches. Soon there were three small lights in our house.
We could not watch television and I could not study. So we sat together on the floor.
My grandmother started telling stories about her childhood. She told us about a flood in 1978 when the water came into their kitchen.
We laughed a lot. My little sister fell asleep on my mother's lap.
At half past nine the lights came back and everybody stood up and went to their own room.
For two hours our house was different.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A small ordinary event given meaning by the last line. Notice that nothing dramatic happens at all.

blocks.heading: 7. The Old Mango Tree
text: There is an old mango tree behind our house. My grandfather planted it before I was born.
It gives fruit in May. The mangoes at the top are the sweetest, but nobody can reach them except the crows.
When I was small I fell from the second branch and broke my arm. My mother said I must never climb it again. I climbed it again the next year.
Last month a storm broke one large branch. My father wanted to cut the tree down because it is old.
My grandmother said no.
The tree is still there. It is leaning a little, but in May there will be mangoes again.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A tree used to hold a family together across three generations. The short sentence "My grandmother said no" stops the story and decides it.

blocks.heading: 8. The Day I Was Late
text: I am never late for school. That is why nobody believed me on Monday.
Our alarm clock did not ring because the electricity was off in the night. I woke up at half past seven.
I did not eat. I put on my uniform, took my bag and ran to the bus halt. The bus had gone.
A man on a motorcycle saw my uniform and stopped. He was my neighbour's brother. He took me to school.
I reached the gate during assembly and stood at the back.
The teacher marked me late anyway.
It was not fair, but I understood. She cannot check every story.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The ending accepts something unfair without complaining about it. That is a mature move a Grade 7 pupil can copy.

blocks.heading: 9. My First Bicycle
text: My bicycle is not new. My cousin used it for four years and then he grew too tall for it.
When my father brought it home the chain was broken and there was rust on the handlebar. We cleaned it together on a Sunday.
Learning to ride was not easy. I fell many times and my knee still has a mark from the third fall.
My father held the seat and ran behind me. One day I turned around and he was standing far away, smiling.
Now I ride to the shop and to my friend's house.
It is old and it makes a noise when I brake. It is the best thing I own.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The moment the father lets go, told without any big words. The last two sentences balance a fault against a feeling.

blocks.heading: 10. The Kind Stranger
text: Last month my mother and I went to the town to buy books. On the way back we could not find our purse.
We had no money for the bus. It was four o'clock and our home is eleven kilometres away.
My mother did not cry but her face changed.
A woman at the bus halt was watching us. She was old and she was selling plantains. She came and gave my mother two hundred rupees.
My mother said she would return it. The woman said, "Somebody helped me once."
We went back the next week with the money. She was not there, and the other sellers did not know her name.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The story does not end tidily, and it is better for it. The stranger's one line explains everything she did.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Ask where the story turns.** Every piece below changes direction once. Finding that moment is the lesson; a story without one is a list.
**Count the sentences, not the words, first.** Ten to fourteen sentences makes a hundred and ten words. A pupil who knows that stops panicking about length.
**Give the dialogue away.** One line of speech lifts a composition. Two pages of it sink one.
**Set a different title from the model** so the class writes rather than remembers.
**Mark two things.** The best sentence, and the one mistake that matters most in that piece.

hero.text: Ten compositions of about 120 words, written at the level a Grade 8 pupil can actually reach - and each one showing a single thing worth copying.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred and twenty words. At this level the paragraph starts to matter: one to set the scene, two or three for what happened, and one to close. A pupil who can plan four paragraphs before writing has learned most of what a composition needs.
The grammar widens a little - *was walking*, *had already gone* - but only where the meaning needs it. There is no new vocabulary a Grade 8 class would have to look up.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 120 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 8 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 128 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. The Flood
text: It rained for three days without stopping. On the third night my father did not sleep. He kept going to the gate with a torch to look at the canal.
At about two o'clock he woke us. The water had already come into the garden. We carried the television, the rice bags and my grandmother's medicine to the upstairs room of our neighbour's house.
By morning the water was above the door handle. We watched our chairs move around the sitting room.
The army came in a boat at eleven and took the old people first.
We lost most of our furniture and all my books. Nobody in our lane was hurt.
When people ask about that week, my father only says we were lucky. I did not understand him then. I do now.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The father's small actions carry the fear - the torch, not sleeping. The last three sentences do the thinking without explaining it.

blocks.heading: 2. A Visit to the Hospital
text: My grandmother fell in the bathroom on a Tuesday and broke her hip. We went to see her the next evening.
The ward was long and full. There were forty beds and the fans were not enough. A baby was crying somewhere near the window.
My grandmother looked smaller than at home. She was wearing a hospital dress and her hair was not combed the way she likes it.
She asked whether I had eaten. I said yes. She asked again after five minutes.
My mother combed her hair for her before we left, and she closed her eyes while it was happening.
Outside, the visitors sat on the wall and waited for the bus in the dark.
I had never thought about how many families are worried on the same evening.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Details instead of feelings: forty beds, the uncombed hair, the same question twice. The last line widens from one family to everybody.

blocks.heading: 3. The Scholarship Class
text: My cousin sat the Grade 5 scholarship examination last year. I watched the whole thing from close by, because she stayed at our house.
She went to a class on Saturday morning, another on Saturday evening, and a third on Sunday. In the week she did papers at night.
By September she knew every kind of question. She also stopped playing.
One evening I found her crying over a paper because she had got thirty-eight out of fifty. Thirty-eight is a good mark.
She passed, and everybody was very happy, and my aunt cried at the temple.
I am glad for her. But I remember the evening with the thirty-eight, and I think somebody should have told her that it was enough.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A composition that takes a position. The writer is happy and uneasy at the same time, and says so - which is harder and better than choosing one.

blocks.heading: 4. My Grandfather's Radio
text: My grandfather has an old radio. It is brown, it has a broken dial, and it is older than my father.
Every morning at half past five he switches it on for the news. He does not turn it loud because the rest of us are sleeping.
Last year the radio stopped working. My uncle brought him a new one with many buttons, and my grandfather thanked him and put it in the cupboard.
Then he took the old radio to a repair shop in the town. The man there said nobody makes that part any more.
My grandfather waited two months. The man found the part somewhere.
Now the news starts at half past five again. My uncle still does not understand it. I think I do.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An object standing in for a person's character. The writer never uses the word stubborn, and does not need to.

blocks.heading: 5. The Day We Painted the Classroom
text: Our classroom walls were grey and marked, so our class teacher asked the principal for permission to paint them.
We collected money for four weeks. Everybody gave something, and two pupils whose families could not give money came on both Saturdays instead.
The painting was harder than we expected. The old paint had to be scraped first, and the dust made everybody cough. My shirt was ruined.
One boy painted a large blue line at the wrong angle near the door. We argued about it for ten minutes and then left it.
On Monday the whole school came to look through our windows.
The line is still there, slightly crooked, above the door. Our class knows exactly who painted it, and we are not telling anybody.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The crooked line is the best thing in the piece. A small imperfection remembered fondly is worth more than a perfect result.

blocks.heading: 6. A Quarrel
text: My friend Dinesh and I did not talk to each other for eleven days.
It started over something small. He told the class that I was afraid of the dark, which was true, and everybody laughed.
I said something worse about his family in front of four people. He went very quiet and walked away.
After that we sat in the same row and looked at different walls. Our friends took sides. At interval I ate alone and pretended I wanted to.
On the twelfth day his sister was ill and he had no money for the bus. I gave him mine.
He said thank you. I said sorry. Neither of us said anything about the eleven days.
What I said was worse than what he said, and he forgave me first.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The writer takes the blame in the last line instead of the first. That delay is what makes the reader trust them.

blocks.heading: 7. The Stray Puppy
text: A brown puppy came to our gate in the rain last August. It was thin and it had a wound on its back leg.
My mother said no. We had no money for a dog and my little brother is afraid of them.
I gave it some rice behind the kitchen, which my mother saw and did not mention.
The next day the rice was on a plate near the step. The day after that there was a piece of fish in it.
On the fourth day my mother washed the wound with warm water and salt while I held the puppy still.
Nobody in our house has ever said that we have a dog. He sleeps under the bench at night and his name is Rocky.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The mother's kindness is shown only through the plate, the fish and the salt water - she never changes her words. Actions against words make a story.

blocks.heading: 8. The School Trip to Sigiriya
text: We left school at four in the morning in two buses. Half the class slept and the other half sang.
Sigiriya is higher than it looks in photographs. The first part was steps, the second part was more steps, and then there were the iron stairs on the side of the rock.
I was afraid there. I held the rail with both hands and did not look down. Our sports teacher walked behind me and talked about cricket the whole way so that I would keep going.
At the top the wind was very strong and you can see for many kilometres.
Coming down took half the time.
I remember the view. I remember the teacher talking about cricket more.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The famous place is the setting; the teacher is the story. Notice how the last two sentences choose what mattered.

blocks.heading: 9. The Mobile Phone
text: There is one mobile phone in our house and it belongs to my father.
During the online classes my sister and I used it together. She has Grade 11 and I have Grade 8, and our classes were sometimes at the same hour.
We made a timetable on paper and stuck it on the wall. It worked for two weeks. After that we started arguing, and my father took the phone to work on Thursdays to stop us.
My sister needed it more than I did. I knew that, and I still argued.
This year we are back in school. The timetable is still on the wall and nobody has taken it down.
Some of my friends had no phone at all. Nobody made a timetable for them.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The last two lines lift a family story into something larger without a speech. That is the whole technique.

blocks.heading: 10. Carrying Water
text: In the dry season the tap in our lane runs for two hours in the morning and nothing comes after that.
My job is the water. I take two buckets and a plastic can to the tap at half past five, and I make three journeys before school.
The queue is the same people every day. The old man from the corner house always tells me to go before him and I always refuse, and then I go before him.
The buckets are not heavy at the tap. They are heavy at our gate.
In June the rain came and the tap ran all day. My mother filled everything in the house anyway, because she does not trust it.
I did not miss the queue. I missed the old man.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: "The buckets are not heavy at the tap. They are heavy at our gate." Two short sentences doing what a paragraph of description could not.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Ask for the four-line plan before the writing.** Situation, what happened, what happened next, how it ended. Ten minutes on the plan saves twenty on the writing.
**Mark the paragraph breaks in one model together.** Ask why each one falls where it does. Most weak compositions at this level are one long paragraph.
**Point out the past continuous when it appears.** *I was walking home when...* is the single most useful pattern for a story, and it is worth one lesson on its own.
**Insist on a real ending.** Not "it was a memorable day" - something that answers the story. Every model below does.
**Read two aloud and compare the openings.** Which one made you want to hear the rest, and what did it do?

hero.text: Ten compositions of about 130 words, written at the level a Grade 9 pupil can actually reach - and each one showing a single thing worth copying.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred and thirty words. This is the year a composition can begin to think as well as describe: something happens, and the writer ends up understanding something they did not understand at the start.
The English is still plain. What has grown is not the vocabulary but the shape - a clear opening, a middle that moves, and a last line that is earned rather than announced.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 130 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 9 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 138 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. The Night of the Storm
text: The wind started at about nine o'clock and by ten it was frightening. We could hear the coconut trees and then something metal moving on a roof somewhere down the lane.
My father put us all in the middle room, the one with no windows. He sat in the doorway with a torch and did not use it.
At some point there was a very loud crack. Nobody said anything for a long moment.
In the morning we saw that the jak tree had fallen across the lane, not on our house. The kitchen roof sheets were in the neighbour's garden. Our gate was bent flat.
By eight o'clock six men were cutting the tree and by noon the lane was open.
I had always thought of our neighbours as people who live near us. That morning I understood that they are something else.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Sound instead of sight - the metal roof, the crack, the silence. The last two sentences name the change without any large words.

blocks.heading: 2. The Prefect Interview
text: Twenty-two of us applied to be prefects and eleven were chosen. The interview was in the principal's office on a Wednesday.
I had prepared answers about discipline and responsibility. I had practised them in front of a mirror, which sounds foolish and was useful.
The principal asked me one question I had not prepared for. He asked what I would do if I saw my own friend breaking a rule.
I said I would report it. He looked at me and said, "Are you telling me the truth, or telling me what I want to hear?"
I thought about it and said I did not know.
I was selected. Two of my friends who gave the confident answer were not.
I still do not know whether I would report Dinesh. I am glad I did not pretend.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An admission of doubt used as the climax. The principal's question, quoted exactly, does more work than any description of him.

blocks.heading: 3. Amma's Sewing Machine
text: My mother's sewing machine stands near the front window because that is where the light is best.
She has had it since before she was married. It is black, it works with a foot pedal, and it makes a sound like a long whisper.
For nineteen years she has sewn school uniforms for the children in our lane. In December and January she works until midnight because school reopens in January and everybody remembers late.
She charges very little. Once I asked her why, and she said that a mother who cannot pay still sends her child to school.
Two years ago my father wanted to buy her an electric machine. She said the old one has never once failed her.
I have grown up to the sound of that machine. When I am away from home I notice the quiet.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A portrait built from work, a price, one line of speech and a sound. The final sentence turns the object into something the writer feels.

blocks.heading: 4. The Boy at the Junction
text: There is a boy who sells newspapers at the junction near my school. He is about my age.
For two years I walked past him every morning and never spoke to him. He had a blue cap and a plastic bag of change and he was always there before me.
In March our teacher gave us an essay on child labour. I wrote four paragraphs about it and got eighteen out of twenty.
That evening I saw him at the junction again and I felt something I did not like.
The next day I bought a paper and asked his name. It is Kavindu. He goes to school in the afternoon session and sells papers in the morning.
He does not need my pity. He was in the top ten of his class last term, which is better than I have ever done.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The essay mark of eighteen out of twenty, set beside the writer's discomfort, is the whole point. The last line refuses the easy ending.

blocks.heading: 5. A Mistake I Made
text: In Grade 8 I copied a friend's mathematics homework for a whole term.
It began once, on a day I had not finished, and then it was easier to keep going than to stop. My marks for homework were good all term. My marks in the term test were not.
The teacher called me after the test. She did not shout. She put my homework book and my answer paper side by side on the table and waited.
I have never felt worse than in that silence.
She made me do the whole term's work again in the holidays, and she checked it herself, page by page.
I was angry with her for about a week. Then I understood that she had given me the holidays instead of giving me a punishment I would have forgotten.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The teacher's silence, and the two books side by side, replace a page of scolding. The last sentence reaches an understanding that takes time.

blocks.heading: 6. The House Next Door
text: An old lady lived alone in the house next to ours. Her children are in Italy and they send money every month.
She used to call me over the wall to help her with small things: a bulb, a jar she could not open, a form she could not read.
I did not always want to go. Sometimes I pretended I had not heard.
In May she was taken to hospital and she did not come back. Her children came for the funeral and stayed for nine days.
The house is locked now. There is a padlock on the gate and the garden has gone wild.
The jar and the bulb took two minutes each. I cannot stop thinking about the times I pretended not to hear, and there is nothing at all that I can do about them now.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Regret written honestly, without asking the reader for forgiveness. Notice how ordinary the things are: a bulb, a jar, a form.

blocks.heading: 7. Losing the Final
text: Our school reached the zonal netball final for the first time in fourteen years. I was in the team.
We trained from half past five every morning for two months. Our coach is a mathematics teacher who played for her university long ago.
In the final we led by four goals at half time. Then their tall girl started scoring and we could not stop her. We lost by two.
In the changing room nobody could speak. Our captain cried, which made it worse, because she never does.
The coach came in and said, "Fourteen years. You are the ones who came back."
There is a photograph of our team in the corridor now, under the word Runners-Up. I walk past it every day and I am not ashamed of it any more.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: "I am not ashamed of it any more" is honest about the time it took. The coach's two short sentences carry the reframing.

blocks.heading: 8. The Letter I Did Not Send
text: When my brother went to Korea to work, I was eleven and I was angry with him.
He had promised to teach me to ride a motorcycle in the April holidays. Instead he left in March with two bags and everybody crying at the gate except me.
I wrote him a letter that week. It was two pages and most of it was unkind. I kept it in my mathematics book and did not post it.
He telephoned every Sunday for three years. He sent the money that built our kitchen and paid for my sister's classes.
He came back in June. He is thinner and he laughs less.
The letter is still in the book. I read it again last month, and I was glad about the only good decision I made when I was eleven.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Restraint as the subject. The writer never describes their own growing up; the unsent letter does it for them.

blocks.heading: 9. The Day the Class Was Quiet
text: Our Sinhala teacher is the strictest in the school and nobody has ever seen her upset.
One Monday she came to class and taught the lesson in a voice we did not know. It was too soft. She did not once ask anybody to stand up.
Somebody had told us before the bell that her mother had died on Saturday.
For forty minutes forty-two pupils sat absolutely still. Nobody passed a note. Nobody asked to go out.
At the end she said, "Thank you, children," and went out quickly.
We talked about it at interval and decided we had done nothing, because we had only sat quietly.
I think now that it was not nothing. Sometimes the only thing you can give a person is one hour in which nobody makes it harder.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A whole class as the character. The last sentence states the idea plainly - which is allowed, once, when the story has earned it.

blocks.heading: 10. Leaving the Village
text: In August my father was transferred and we moved to Gampaha. I had lived in the same village for fourteen years.
The packing took four days. Our house looked much bigger empty, and much smaller than I remembered at the same time.
My friends came on the last evening. We did not do anything special. We sat on the culvert as usual and talked about nothing, and then it got dark and they went home.
In the lorry I did not look back, because I had decided in advance not to.
Gampaha is better in most ways. The school is bigger, the bus comes every ten minutes, and there is a library.
I have made friends here and I like them. But nobody in this town knows what I was like when I was six.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The ending concedes that the new place is better and still mourns the old one. Holding two true things at once is real writing.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Cover the last two lines and ask the class to write them.** Then compare. This is the single most useful exercise with a model at this level.
**Ask what the writer believed at the beginning and at the end.** If nothing changed, the piece is a report, not a story.
**Ban the phrase "it was a memorable day".** It is what a pupil writes instead of an ending. None of these use it.
**Look at where the short sentences fall.** They are almost always at the moment of greatest weight. Length is a tool, not an accident.
**Set one of these titles as a speaking task first.** A pupil who has told the story aloud writes it twice as well.

hero.text: Ten compositions of about 140 words, written at the level a Grade 10 pupil can actually reach - and each one showing a single thing worth copying.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred and forty words. This is the year the Ordinary Level work begins, and these are built the way an examination answer has to be built: an opening that wastes nothing, a middle with one clear line through it, and an ending that answers the beginning.
Two of the ten put an opinion rather than tell a story, because the O/L paper asks for that as well. The English remains within reach of a second-language learner at this grade.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 140 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 10 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 143 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. The Work My Father Does
text: My father is a mason. He builds walls, plasters them, and lays floor tiles, and he has done it since he was seventeen.
He leaves the house at six and comes back after six. In the evening there is cement dust in his hair and on his eyebrows, and he washes at the tap outside before he comes in.
For years I did not tell people at school what he does. Some boys in my class have fathers with offices.
In April he took me to a site because his helper was ill. I carried mortar for six hours. By noon my hands were bleeding at the base of the fingers.
He does that six days a week and then asks me whether I have finished my homework.
I tell people what my father does now. I say it first, before they ask.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The change is shown by a habit, not a statement - he used to hide it, now he says it first. Six hours of carrying mortar is worth more than any adjective.

blocks.heading: 2. The Year of the Examination
text: In Grade 11 the year is not a year. It is a countdown, and everybody in the house is counting.
My timetable is on the almariah door. School until half past one, classes on four evenings, papers on Sunday morning. My mother wakes me at four in the last two months.
The worst part is not the work. It is that everybody asks the same question. Relatives telephone to ask how the studies are going, and the only answer they will accept is that they are going well.
I am doing nine subjects. I will probably do well in six of them.
What I want to say, and cannot, is that I am not lazy and I am not confident either, and both of those things are allowed to be true at the same time.
In December it will be over. I am told that nobody remembers the marks afterwards.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An honest account of pressure that never asks for sympathy. The sentence about two things being true at once is the kind of thinking O/L examiners reward.

blocks.heading: 3. A Decision I Had to Make
text: Last year I was selected for the school cricket pool and for the English Day debating team. The practices were on the same three evenings.
I wanted cricket. I am not good enough to play for a district, and I knew that even then.
My English teacher did not tell me what to choose. She asked me one question: which one would I still be glad about in five years?
I chose debating, and for about a month I regretted it every time I saw the nets from the corridor.

We won the zonal round and lost the provincial one. I spoke for four minutes in front of two hundred people, and afterwards a girl from another school told me my second point was the strongest of the day.
I still watch cricket. I am not sorry. But it was not an easy choice and I dislike stories that pretend such choices are easy.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A composition about choosing that admits the cost of the choice. The teacher's single question does the persuading, so the writer never has to lecture.

blocks.heading: 4. The Tuition Bus
text: The tuition bus leaves the junction at half past three and comes back at half past eight.
There are forty of us from six schools. Everybody has a bag and a bottle of water and nobody has energy. For the first ten minutes nobody speaks at all.

By the second week of any term the seats are settled. The Grade 11 pupils sit at the back. There is always one boy who sleeps with his mouth open and one girl who studies the whole way, holding the notes above her knees.
On the way back the bus is different. The windows are down, somebody plays music from a telephone, and the tiredness turns into a strange kind of cheerfulness.
I have learned less English in that class than my parents hope and more on that bus than they would believe.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A place observed closely - the settled seats, the boy asleep, the girl studying. The last line earns a laugh and makes a point in one sentence.

blocks.heading: 5. Working in the Holidays
text: In the August holidays I worked in my uncle's hardware shop for three weeks. He paid me a thousand rupees a week.
The work was mostly lifting. Cement, paint tins, coils of wire, forty-kilogram bags that two of us carried between us.

What I did not expect was the talking. Customers want to explain their whole building before they buy a bolt. By the second week I could tell which man had already been to three shops and which one had decided before he came in.
On the last day my uncle gave me three thousand rupees and a fourth note on top of it.
I bought my mother a pair of slippers and I put the rest away.
Three thousand rupees is not a great deal of money. I have never spent anything as carefully since.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Specific money, specific weight, specific days. The observation about customers shows the writer learning something nobody taught them.

blocks.heading: 6. The Girl Who Stopped Coming
text: Sixty-one pupils were in our class in January. In August there were fifty-eight.
One of the three was Ishara, who sat two rows in front of me. She was good at science and she laughed at things before the rest of us understood them.
Her father lost his job at the garment factory in May. In June she was absent on Mondays, then on Mondays and Fridays, and in July she stopped coming.
Our class teacher went to the house twice. The second time, Ishara was there and she was looking after her two younger brothers.
Somebody said she would come back next term. She did not.
We talk about the pupils who fail the examination. Nobody counts the ones who never get to sit it, and our register that year counted three.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The numbers frame the whole piece - sixty-one, fifty-eight, three. A social point made through one named person is stronger than any general statement.

blocks.heading: 7. Our Class Photograph
text: The photograph was taken in February on the steps of the main hall. Four rows, sixty-one of us, the teachers in the middle.
It took twenty minutes because somebody was always blinking or talking. Our class teacher said "last time" four times.
I have the copy in my file. In it I am in the third row, slightly behind a taller boy, and my tie is crooked.
What I notice now is not myself. It is that everybody in that picture was still in school, and two years later we are in eleven different places.
Three are abroad. One is married. Two, including the boy in front of me, I have not been able to find at all.
A photograph is not a record of a day. It is a record of a day being the last one of something.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The final two sentences turn an ordinary object into an idea. That move - object, detail, then meaning - is one a pupil can use on any topic.

blocks.heading: 8. The Long Walk Home
text: The bus strike began at noon and by two o'clock it was clear that nothing was running.
Our school is eleven kilometres from my house. Four of us started walking together at half past two.
The first five kilometres were almost enjoyable. We bought ice palam at a shop and complained about the heat and a teacher.
After that the road turned uphill and nobody talked much. My shoes are school shoes, not walking shoes, and by the seventh kilometre I could feel every stone.
At the eighth kilometre a lorry carrying sand stopped for us without being asked, and we rode the last three standing in the back.
I reached home at half past five, filthy and very thirsty.
I have taken that bus four hundred times and remember none of the journeys. I remember all eleven kilometres.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The kilometres give the piece its structure - five, seven, eight, three. The ending explains why the story was worth telling at all.

blocks.heading: 9. Should Pupils Be Allowed Mobile Phones in School?
text: Most schools in Sri Lanka do not allow pupils to bring mobile telephones, and I think that rule is right, although not for the reason usually given.
The argument we are given is that telephones are a distraction. That is true, but a distracted pupil will find a window to look out of.

The real reason is fairness. In my class some pupils have telephones worth more than a month of my father's pay and some have none at all. During the online classes we all saw what that difference does. In school, at least, the uniform hides it.
Against the rule there is one serious point: a girl travelling home at night is safer with a telephone.
So the sensible rule is not a ban but a locked drawer in the office, handed back at the end of the day.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An opinion piece that states the common argument, sets it aside, gives a better one, admits the other side and lands on a practical answer.

blocks.heading: 10. Is Reading Still Worth the Time?
text: My cousin says that nobody needs to read books any more, because anything a book can tell you can be watched in twelve minutes.
He is partly right. For facts, he is entirely right. If I want to know how an engine works, a film will teach me faster than a chapter.

But a book does something a film cannot. It makes you build the picture yourself, which is slow and is exactly the point. A reader spends four hours inside another person's head and comes out slightly different.
There is also the plain matter of examinations. Pupils who read write better, and every teacher I know can tell within a page which pupils read.
I am not going to claim that books are dying or that they will save anybody. I will only say that twelve minutes buys information, and four hours buys something else.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It concedes the strongest point against it in the second paragraph. A pupil who learns to do that early will write good discursive essays for years.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Time them.** At O/L a composition of this length has to be planned, written and checked in about twenty-five minutes. A model read in comfort teaches nothing about that.
**Make them find the line through it.** Every piece below can be summed up in one sentence. A pupil who cannot state that sentence before writing will wander.
**Use the last five minutes on checking, always.** Tense, subject-verb agreement, full stops. Marks are lost there, not on ideas.
**Compare a narrative and an opinion piece from the list.** The paragraph shapes are different, and pupils who see the difference stop writing stories when they are asked for arguments.
**Do not let them memorise one composition for the examination.** A memorised piece bent to fit a different question loses more marks than a plain honest answer.

hero.text: Ten compositions of about 165 words, written at the level a Grade 11 pupil can actually reach - and each one showing a single thing worth copying.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model compositions of about a hundred and sixty-five words, at Ordinary Level standard. The set mixes the three kinds of writing the paper actually asks for: narrative, description, and an opinion argued out.

That mixture is deliberate. A class that has only practised stories loses marks the moment the question asks what they think, and a class that has only practised arguments writes stories with no life in them. Four here are narrative, three describe, and three take a position.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 165 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 11 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 162 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. The Day I Had to Speak
text: I was told on a Thursday that I would give the vote of thanks at the prize-giving on Saturday. The pupil who was to do it had chickenpox.
I am not a confident speaker. In class I answer questions in six words and sit down.
My English teacher wrote the speech with me on Friday afternoon, and then made me say it eleven times. The eleventh time she stopped correcting me and only listened.
On Saturday the hall held about six hundred people. The chief guest was a doctor from Colombo. I could hear my own voice in the microphone, half a second behind me, which nobody had warned me about.
I forgot one sentence in the middle. I do not think anybody except my teacher knew.
Afterwards three teachers said well done and my mother cried in the car park, which was embarrassing and also not.
I am still not a confident speaker. But I know now that being frightened and doing it anyway are not opposites.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The echo in the microphone is the detail that proves the writer was there. The last sentence refuses a fake transformation and is stronger for it.

blocks.heading: 2. My Grandmother's Kitchen
text: My grandmother's kitchen is at the back of the house, down two steps, and it is darker than any other room.

The walls above the hearth are black from forty years of smoke. There is a shelf of glass bottles with no labels, and she knows what is in every one of them. The coconut scraper is screwed to a low stool and the handle has worn smooth and pale where her hand goes.
It smells of three things at once: woodsmoke, coconut oil, and the dried fish that hangs in a basket near the window.
She cooks sitting down. Everything she needs is within the reach of an arm, because she arranged it that way long before her knees gave trouble.
My mother's kitchen has tiles, a gas cooker and a window that opens properly. It is a better kitchen in every way that can be written down.
Nothing cooked in it has ever tasted the same.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Description through wear and smell, not adjectives: the pale handle, the unlabelled bottles. The comparison at the end gives the description a purpose.

blocks.heading: 3. The Examination Hall
text: The hall is the school gymnasium with the nets taken down. There are two hundred and forty desks in twelve rows, each one with a number card stuck to the corner.
It is very quiet before an examination, and it is the wrong kind of quiet. Two hundred people breathing and nobody speaking. Somebody's shoe taps. A fan clicks each time it turns.
The invigilator walks up and down the row and his shoes are the loudest thing in the building.
When the papers come round face down, everybody reads the number on the card again, which is pointless because it has not changed.
Then the bell, and the sound of two hundred and forty papers turning at once, which is like one long breath.
After that the hall is not frightening any more. It is only a room where you have three hours and some questions.
It is the fifteen minutes before the bell that nobody prepares you for.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Sound builds the whole description - the tapping shoe, the fan, the papers turning. The final line tells you what the piece was really about.

blocks.heading: 4. The Three-Wheel Driver
text: Mr Ranjith has parked at our junction for nineteen years. He is the person our lane telephones at two in the morning.

He took my grandmother to hospital in 2019 and waited outside until four o'clock without being asked. He has taken pupils from our lane to the O/L examination hall every year for as long as I can remember, and he does not charge for that.
He knows every shortcut between here and the town. He also knows which houses are having difficulty, and he says nothing about it to anybody.
During the fuel queues in 2022 he stood for nine hours and then used what he had for a woman who needed dialysis twice a week.
He is not a rich man. His three-wheeler is old and the back seat is patched with grey tape.
People talk about wanting to serve the country. Mr Ranjith has never once used that word, and I can name eleven people in our lane who owe him something.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A character built entirely out of what he has done, ending with a quiet contrast between talking and doing. Note that the writer never calls him kind.

blocks.heading: 5. The Last Day of School
text: Our last day was a Friday in November, eleven days before the examination began.
There was no ceremony. The timetable said Sinhala, mathematics and two periods of revision, and that is what happened.

At interval somebody produced a marker pen and started signing shirts, which is not allowed, and by the end of the day about forty of us were wearing our whole class on our backs. Our class teacher saw it and went back into the staff room without saying anything.
The last bell rang at half past one as it has rung four thousand times.
Nobody wanted to leave the classroom. We stood in it for twenty minutes talking about the examination because it was easier than talking about anything else.
I walked out of the gate at two o'clock with my bag on one shoulder.
I had been through that gate twice a day for eleven years. It is a perfectly ordinary gate and I have never looked at it properly since.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The teacher who walks away rather than enforce the rule, and the twenty minutes of talking about the wrong thing. Both show feeling without naming it.

blocks.heading: 6. The Aeroplane in April
text: My mother left for Kuwait on the nineteenth of April. She is a housemaid there and her contract is for two years.
We went to Katunayake in my uncle's van, seven of us, and we reached at eleven at night for a flight at four in the morning.
The departure area has a glass wall. She stood on the other side of it for a long time and we stood on this side, and after a while there was nothing left to say and nobody would go first.
My father did not speak in the van coming back.
She calls on Sunday mornings. The kitchen is finished now and my sister is in a nursing course, and both of those things are because of Kuwait.
When people say that our country sends its mothers away, I know they are right.
I also know that our kitchen has a roof, and I have not worked out how to hold those two facts at the same time.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Two true things that do not resolve. An ending that admits it cannot resolve them is honest writing, and examiners notice it.

blocks.heading: 7. The Perahera
text: The perahera passes our lane on the full moon day in August, and people take their places on the wall two hours early.

It comes first as sound: the drums from somewhere near the junction, before anything can be seen. Then the whip-crackers, and the smell of the coconut-oil torches, which is heavy and sweet and gets into your clothes.
The dancers come in lines, their silver headpieces catching the torchlight, and the drummers walk with their heads tipped slightly back.
The elephants come last and they change the street. People who have been shouting stop shouting. You can hear the chains and the feet, which make almost no noise at all for something so large.
It takes about forty minutes to pass and the lane smells of oil until the morning.
Small children are carried home asleep on shoulders. I was carried home from this perahera myself, and I do not remember which year I was last carried.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The order of the senses - sound, smell, then sight - is how a procession actually arrives. The last sentence makes it personal in nine words.

blocks.heading: 8. Does Failure Teach Anything?
text: We are often told that failure is a good teacher. I think that is true only under one condition, and the condition is usually left out.
I failed mathematics in the second term of Grade 10. Thirty-four marks. It taught me nothing at all for about two months, because all I felt was shame, and shame does not teach, it only silences.
What changed was not the failure. It was a teacher who sat with my paper and showed me that twenty-two of my lost marks came from three kinds of mistake, all of them fixable.
After that the failure became useful, because it had become information.
So failure by itself teaches very little. Failure plus somebody who will explain it teaches a great deal.
This matters because we tell pupils to learn from their mistakes and then leave them alone with the paper. A pupil alone with a bad mark does not learn. A pupil shown where the marks went does.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It takes a saying everyone accepts and adds the missing condition. One number - thirty-four - makes the argument concrete instead of theoretical.

blocks.heading: 9. Whose Choice Is My Career?
text: My parents want me to do science for the Advanced Level. I want to do arts, and specifically English and geography.

Their reasons are not foolish. They have watched cousins finish arts degrees and sit at home for three years afterwards, and they are frightened of that for me. When people say Sri Lankan parents only care about status, they are being unfair to my father, who is afraid of something real.
My reason is simpler and harder to defend: I am good at these subjects and I am not good at chemistry.

We have not settled it. What has helped is that I stopped arguing about which stream is better and started finding out what somebody with my subjects actually does for a living, with names and salaries.
That changed the conversation, because it turned my wish into a plan.
A seventeen-year-old asking to be trusted should expect to be asked what the plan is.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It argues its own case while treating the other side fairly - a very high-scoring move. The last line concedes something without giving up the position.

blocks.heading: 10. The Rubbish at the End of Our Lane
text: At the end of our lane, where the culvert crosses the drain, there is a pile of rubbish that has been there for as long as I can remember.

Nobody decided to put it there. One person left a bag, and then the place became a place where bags are left. It is now about the size of a small car and it smells for twenty metres in either direction.
The council lorry comes on Tuesdays and it does not come down our lane, because the lane is too narrow for it to turn.
In 2023 some of us cleared it. Forty bags. It was clean for five weeks.
I used to think the problem was that people do not care. I no longer think that. The people who leave bags there also sweep their own gardens every morning.
The problem is that the lorry cannot turn, and nobody has ever been given anywhere else to put it.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An environmental piece that resists blaming people and finds the actual cause. Forty bags and five weeks make the argument impossible to dismiss.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Name the type before reading each one.** Story, description, opinion. Pupils who cannot tell which is being asked for answer the wrong question under pressure.
**Give them the plan, not the piece.** Four lines of plan for each model, written on the board, is a better lesson than the finished composition.
**In the opinion pieces, find the concession.** Each one admits the other side once. Examiners reward that; pupils almost never do it unprompted.
**Practise the opening sentence on its own.** Ten pupils, ten openings for the same title, read aloud. It takes fifteen minutes and it changes how they start.
**Insist on the last five minutes for checking.** At this level the commonest lost marks are tense slips and missing full stops, not weak ideas.
