blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model essays of about two hundred and fifty words - the length an Advanced Level General English answer runs to. Seven argue a position and three reflect on something that happened.

One rule was followed throughout: no national statistics. An essay that leans on a figure teaches pupils to quote numbers they cannot check, and a figure invented under examination pressure costs more than it gains. The evidence in these is observation and reasoning, which is what a candidate actually has in the hall.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 250 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 12 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 252 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. Why Everyone Says They Want English
text: Ask any parent in my town what they want for their child and English will be in the first three answers. Ask what they mean by it and the answers scatter. That gap is worth examining, because we are all pursuing something we have not defined.

For some, English is a job requirement, and they are simply right. A great many advertised positions ask for it, often for work in which very little English is actually used. The requirement functions less as a skill test than as a filter.
For others, English is respect. A person who speaks it is spoken to differently in a bank, a hospital and a government office. This is the part nobody puts in writing and everybody has seen.

The difficulty is that these two wants pull in different directions. English as a job requirement means functional competence - emails, telephone calls, instructions understood the first time. English as respect means accent and confidence, which are far harder to teach and far more easily faked.
Our teaching mostly serves neither. A pupil who has spent eleven years on grammar exercises can name a tense and cannot ask a stranger for directions.

If we are honest about which of the two we are aiming at, the teaching follows. Functional English is teachable in a classroom with forty pupils and no equipment. The other thing is not, and pretending otherwise is why so many leave school having studied English for a decade and unable to use it.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It begins by identifying a confusion rather than taking a side, then separates two meanings and shows they need different teaching. Defining the question is often the whole essay.

blocks.heading: 2. The First Month in the Advanced Level Class
text: Nobody warns you that the Advanced Level is not a harder version of the Ordinary Level. It is a different activity with the same furniture.

In the first week our chemistry teacher said something I did not understand at all, and then said it again in a different way, and I understood it. In the second week the same thing happened and I did not understand it the second time either. That was new. At O/L I had never met a sentence I could not eventually memorise my way past.

The class itself is smaller - eleven of us, instead of sixty-one - and that changes everything. There is nowhere to hide. If I have not read the chapter, the teacher knows within four minutes, and not because she is checking.

The other change is time. There is a great deal of it and none of it is organised for you. At O/L the timetable did the deciding. Now there are free periods, and a free period is a test of something the school has never taught us.
I have wasted most of them so far. I say that plainly because pretending otherwise would make this essay useless.

What I have worked out is small but it is real: I understand a chapter when I can explain it to somebody who has not read it, and not before. Reading it four times proves nothing. Saying it once out loud proves everything.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A reflective essay that admits failure in the middle and ends with one usable conclusion rather than a resolution. The eleven-versus-sixty-one contrast does a paragraph's work in a clause.

blocks.heading: 3. Has Social Media Changed the Way We Read?
text: The complaint is familiar: young people cannot read any more, and the telephone is to blame. I read more words in a day than my father did at my age, so the complaint as stated is plainly false. Something has changed, though, and it is worth naming accurately.

What has changed is not the quantity of reading but its shape. A page of print asks you to hold an argument in mind for three or four minutes. A feed asks you to hold nothing at all, because the next item is unrelated to the last. Both are reading. Only one builds the habit of following a thought that does not immediately reward you.

I notice this in myself when I study. A dense paragraph produces a physical impatience that has nothing to do with difficulty - I understand it, I simply want it to be over. That impatience is learned, and I did not have it three years ago.

In fairness, the feed has given us things the book could not. I have read writing by people whose books would never have reached my town, and arguments from three countries about the same event on the same morning. That is a real gain and the people who complain rarely admit it.

The honest conclusion is not that one is good and one is bad. It is that the two train different muscles, and school is now the only place where the slower one is trained at all. That makes what happens in a literature period more important than it was, not less.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It rejects the popular claim, then finds the true version underneath it. The paragraph of self-observation is what lifts this above a general opinion.

blocks.heading: 4. Should Free University Education Continue?
text: The free university system is the one thing about our country that almost everybody defends, and the defence is usually made badly - by feeling rather than by argument. It deserves better, because it is defensible.

The case against it is serious and should be stated properly. Places are limited and demand is not, so a system that is free at the point of use still excludes the great majority who do not get in. Worse, the pupils who do get in are disproportionately those whose families could afford years of private tuition. Public money therefore subsidises the best-prepared, which is not what free education was for.
That is a real objection and it is an argument for reform, not for fees.

The reason fees would not fix it is that the barrier they would remove is not the barrier that is doing the damage. A bright child in my district is lost long before university - at the Grade 5 examination, or when a school has no chemistry teacher for two years, or when a mother goes abroad and the eldest daughter starts cooking. Charging that child's more fortunate classmate would not reach her.
So the question is placed wrongly when it is asked as free or paid. The money and the attention belong earlier, in the schools that feed the system rather than the institution at the end of it.
Defend free education by all means. But defending it while ignoring the schools is defending a door while the corridor to it is collapsing.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It gives the opposing case a full paragraph and calls it serious, then shows the question itself is misframed. The closing image earns its place because the argument built to it.

blocks.heading: 5. The Village I Will Probably Leave
text: There are three ways to earn a living in my village: the paddy, the government, or leaving. Everybody in my class knows this, and nobody says it at home.

I am in the science stream, which means I have already chosen the third. There is no laboratory work here and no employer who needs it. If the results are good I will go to a university in another province and then to a city, and I will come back for New Year and funerals.

What makes this uncomfortable is not the leaving. It is that the village paid for it. My primary teacher stayed after school for nothing. The temple gave books. When my father was ill the lane found money in four days without being asked. Every one of those people knows they were investing in somebody's departure, and they did it anyway.
People talk about the brain drain as though it were a betrayal. From the inside it looks less like betrayal and more like the plan working exactly as intended.
I do not have a clean answer. I know that my going will help my family and will take one more educated person out of a place that has few. Both of those are true and neither cancels the other.

The least I can do is be accurate about it. I am not going away to serve the village. I am going because there is nothing here for what I have been trained to do, and the people who trained me knew that first.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Reflective writing with an uncomfortable honesty and no false resolution. The line about investing in a departure is the whole essay in one sentence.

blocks.heading: 6. What the Shramadana Taught Me
text: Our school society organised a shramadana at the district hospital in the August holidays: fourteen pupils, two teachers, one Saturday, and the job of clearing and painting the boundary wall of the children's ward.
I went because a friend was going. I want to record that honestly, because the essays about volunteering always begin with somebody wanting to serve, and that was not my reason.

The work was unglamorous. The first three hours were not painting but removing what was behind the wall - bottles, bags, a bicycle frame, and a great deal of broken glass that had to be picked out by hand. Nobody had photographed that part when the society advertised the event.

What changed my view was not the painting. It was a nurse who came out at about eleven with tea for all of us and said that she had asked for the wall to be cleared four times. The problem had never been that nobody cared. It was that nobody whose job it was had a Saturday and fourteen people.
I had assumed, without examining it, that neglected places are neglected because of indifference. Mostly they are neglected because the people who mind are already working.
The wall is yellow now and it will need doing again in three years. We did not solve anything.
But I stopped being a person who thinks a problem is explained once somebody has been blamed for it, and that is a larger change than a wall.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It begins by admitting an unflattering motive, which buys the reader's trust for everything after. The nurse's four requests reframe the whole piece.

blocks.heading: 7. The Trouble with Tuition
text: Almost every pupil in my class attends private classes, including the pupils who are taught the same subject by the same teacher in school. Stated plainly like that, the system is obviously strange. Lived from inside, it feels unavoidable, and understanding why is more useful than condemning it.

The usual accusation is that teachers teach badly in school in order to sell classes in the evening. I have had eleven teachers this year and I believe that of none of them. The truth is duller. A syllabus written for a certain number of periods meets a school year that loses weeks to examinations, sports meets, holidays and absent staff, and the arithmetic does not work. The private class is where the missing weeks are bought back.
That explains it. It does not excuse what follows.

What follows is that a pupil's results now depend on a payment, and everybody has agreed to stop noticing. A child whose family cannot pay four thousand rupees a month is not competing in the same examination as I am, whatever the paper says. We call the result merit.

There is also a cost to those of us who can pay. I am in a classroom from seven in the morning until eight at night, and I have not read a book that was not a textbook for two years. Whatever that is producing, it is not education.
The honest reform is boring: make the school year actually contain the syllabus. Nobody campaigns for that, because it sounds like nothing.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It refuses the popular villain, finds a structural cause, and then insists the cause does not excuse the harm. The last paragraph shows an unexciting answer can be the right one.

blocks.heading: 8. The Year My Grandfather Stopped Talking
text: My grandfather had a stroke in February. The speech went and most of the right side went with it.

He had been a talker. He read three newspapers and argued with all of them. In the first weeks after he came home from hospital he tried to speak and produced sounds that were not words, and then he stopped trying in front of visitors.

The therapy was in the town, twice a week, and my mother took him on the bus because a three-wheeler twice a week was not possible for a year. He worked at it the way he had done everything, which is to say stubbornly and without complaining.
By August he had about forty words. He has more now. They are not always the words he wants, and the wrong word arrives with complete confidence, which is the cruellest part of it.
What I did not expect is how much he communicates without them. He has a particular way of tapping the arm of the chair twice that means he disagrees, and every one of us knows it.
I used to think of language as the thing that carries a person's mind to other people. Watching him has taught me it is one of several vehicles, and not the one we notice losing.
He still gets the newspaper every morning. He reads it slowly and he taps the chair twice, and we all know exactly what he means.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A difficult subject handled without sentimentality. The repeated detail of the two taps opens and closes the essay, which gives it a shape a reader feels rather than notices.

blocks.heading: 9. Are Examinations a Fair Measure?
text: Every year somebody argues that examinations measure only memory. Every year the argument is popular and goes nowhere, and it goes nowhere because it is half true and offered as though it were wholly true.

What an examination genuinely measures is performance under time pressure with no help available. That is a real skill and it is not nothing: a doctor deciding in four minutes, an engineer checking a figure at midnight. The people who dismiss examinations rarely explain what they would put in place that could be marked fairly for hundreds of thousands of candidates by people who do not know them.

That last condition is the one the critics skip. Coursework and continuous assessment measure more of what matters, and they measure it through a teacher who can be pressured, and a family who can pay somebody to help. An anonymous three-hour paper is crude precisely because it is incorruptible.

So the fair criticism is not that examinations measure the wrong thing. It is that we allow them to measure the only thing. A pupil who cannot write quickly under pressure is judged to have understood nothing, and we all know pupils of whom that is untrue.

The sensible position is unexciting again: keep the anonymous paper, and stop treating it as a complete account of a person. That means universities looking at more than one number, and it means adults stopping the habit of asking a seventeen-year-old what their results were as though it settled the question of who they are.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It defends the thing it is expected to attack, then finds the criticism that survives. Naming what the other side skips is one of the strongest moves in argument.

blocks.heading: 10. The Farmer Next Door and the Changing Rain
text: Mr Wijesuriya has farmed the two acres behind our house for thirty-one years, and he decides when to sow by watching the sky. For most of those years that worked.

He says now that the rain has stopped keeping its appointments. Not that there is less of it - that it comes in the wrong weeks and then comes all at once. Three years ago he sowed on the day he had sowed for a decade and it did not rain for five weeks. Last year it rained so hard in the third week that the seed was washed into the drain.
I am careful about what I claim from this. One farmer's thirty-one years beside one field is not evidence about a planet, and an essay that turns his observation into a statistic would be dishonest.

But it is evidence about something. It is evidence that the knowledge he holds - which is real knowledge, built by repetition and unwritten - is losing its predictive value, and that nothing is being offered to replace it. He cannot read a forecast in English. The one on the radio covers a province, and his decision is about a field.

The public argument about the climate is conducted between people who will read about the consequences. The decisions are being made by people watching the sky at five in the morning with no better information than their grandfathers had.
Whatever else is required, that gap is closeable now, and closing it needs no international agreement at all.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It states the limits of its own evidence in the middle paragraph, which makes everything around it more credible - and then finds the argument the evidence does support.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Find the thesis sentence in each one.** It is usually at the end of the first paragraph. An essay whose position cannot be located in one sentence has not got one.
**Find the concession.** Every argument here gives the other side its best point, in full, and then answers it. This is the difference between an essay and a complaint.
**Count the paragraphs, then the words per paragraph.** Two hundred and fifty words is four or five paragraphs. Pupils who write nine have written a list.
**Make them argue the opposite side of one of these.** Fifteen minutes, spoken, no notes. It exposes immediately whether they understood the argument or memorised it.
**Discuss the no-statistics rule with them openly.** Candidates lose credibility on invented figures more often than teachers realise, and reasoning is always available.

blocks.heading: About these models
text: Ten model essays of about two hundred and fifty words, written at the point where the Advanced Level examination is months away rather than years. The length is the same as Grade 12; the demand is not.

These commit to a position inside the first paragraph, waste no sentence on introduction, and several of them answer a question as it would be set on a paper rather than a topic the writer chose. As in Grade 12, no national statistics are quoted - the reasoning has to carry the essay, because in the hall that is all a candidate has.

blocks.title: Ten compositions, about 250 words each
text: Every piece below was written to the length a Grade 13 pupil is expected to manage - the ten average 255 words. They are RCF English's own work, free to print, read aloud or put on a screen.

blocks.heading: 1. Should Students Be Allowed to Use Artificial Intelligence?
text: The question is usually asked as though a rule could settle it. It cannot, because the honest answer depends entirely on what the pupil is being asked to do, and we have not sorted our assignments into the two kinds that matter.

Some school work exists to produce a document. A summary of a chapter, a list of causes, a neat paragraph on a set topic - the value is in the artefact, and a machine that produces it faster is simply a better tool, in the way a calculator is.

Other work exists to change the pupil. An essay is not wanted because the world needs another essay. It is wanted because the act of writing it forces a mind to order itself, and that ordering is the entire point. Handing that to a machine is not cheating so much as declining the lesson while attending the class.
The trouble is that these two kinds of task look identical on a worksheet, and we have been setting them interchangeably for years without noticing.
So a ban is the wrong instrument. It cannot be enforced, and enforcing it would waste the one genuinely useful tool a pupil in a school without a library now has.

What is required is duller and harder: teachers deciding, task by task, whether a given piece of work is for the document or for the pupil, and saying which. A class told why a rule exists will mostly keep it. A class told only that a rule exists will route around it by March.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It refuses the yes-or-no framing and replaces it with a distinction that does the work. Notice that the conclusion asks something of teachers, not of the machine.

blocks.heading: 2. Why Do Employers Ask for English?
text: A great many advertisements in this country ask for fluency in English for work in which almost no English is spoken. This is worth explaining rather than resenting, because the explanation changes what a candidate should do about it.

The first reason is genuine. Suppliers, software, manuals, regulations and the head office may all be in English, and a person who cannot read them cannot be trusted with a decision. For those posts the requirement is not a barrier, it is the job.

The second reason is that English is being used as a proxy. An employer with three hundred applications and no time reaches for something that correlates with schooling, city upbringing and confidence with strangers. English does correlate with all three. It is a lazy filter, and it is not irrational - which is exactly why it will not be abandoned because it is unfair.
The consequence for an applicant is uncomfortable but clear. Complaining about the second reason is correct and will not get anybody employed. The filter has to be passed.

The consequence for the rest of us is larger. Every year, capable people are removed from consideration for work they could do well, on a criterion nobody in the interview room could defend in writing. That is a waste the country pays for twice: once in the person's lost income, and once in the position filled by somebody less able who happened to have the language.
Neither fact is a reason to stop learning English. Both are reasons to stop pretending the requirement is always about the work.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It separates the legitimate reason from the lazy one, then gives the practical conclusion and the public one separately. Refusing to let the reader off with indignation is what makes it mature.

blocks.heading: 3. Why Young People Want to Leave
text: Ask a Grade 13 class how many intend to work abroad and the hands go up before the question is finished. In my class it is most of us. The usual explanation is money, and money is in it, but money alone does not explain why the wish is held so calmly.

The calmness is the part worth examining. My parents' generation regarded going abroad as a sacrifice - something undertaken for a house or a sister's wedding, with the intention of returning. We regard it as a career step, which is a different thing entirely.

What changed is not our patriotism. It is our estimate of how long things take here. A person who watches a queue for three years stops asking whether it will move and starts asking how to get out of it. Every young person I know has a story of that kind: a certificate that took eight months, an appointment made and postponed twice, a qualified relative who waited four years for a posting.
It would be comfortable to conclude with a sentence about serving the nation. I do not believe it and neither would anybody reading this.

What I do believe is that the wish to leave is not a feeling about the country. It is a judgement about predictability, and it would be changed by nothing more romantic than institutions that did what they said within the time they said.
That is not sentimentality. It is the only thing on the list that would actually work.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It identifies the wrong explanation, finds the real variable, and then refuses the patriotic ending it could easily have written. The refusal is the strongest paragraph.

blocks.heading: 4. Waiting for the Results
text: The results come out at some point between four and six months after the last paper, and nobody will tell you which day. That interval is a stranger thing than the examination.

For the first fortnight I did what everybody does, which is to reconstruct the papers from memory and mark them. This is a thoroughly useless activity and I could not stop. I worked out that I had almost certainly lost eleven marks on one question, and I revisited that eleven for weeks, as though the number could still be negotiated.
Then the reconstruction stopped working, because I began to forget the questions.

What is difficult about the wait is not anxiety, exactly. It is being suspended - unable to plan, because three different futures each require a different decision, and unable to rest, because a result is coming that will be spoken about for years. My relatives have already asked twice. My mother has stopped asking, which is its own kind of pressure.

I have started working in the mornings at a computer shop in the town. It pays very little and it has been the most useful part of the wait, because it is the first thing in three years that nobody will grade.

I do not know what the results will say. I have noticed something I did not expect, though: after the first month, the person waiting is no longer the person who sat the paper, and it seems unjust that the envelope will only have news about him.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A precise account of a state most candidates live through and never describe. The eleven marks, revisited for weeks, is the detail that makes it recognisable.

blocks.heading: 5. Is Public Transport Worth Investing In?
text: The argument for spending on buses and trains is usually made in the language of congestion, and it is the weakest form of the case. Congestion annoys the people who already have vehicles. The stronger case is about the people who do not.

Consider what a bus timetable decides. It decides which schools a child can attend, how far from home a woman can accept work, and whether a farmer's produce reaches a market or is sold at the gate for whatever is offered. A household without a vehicle has its possibilities drawn for it by somebody else's route map, and most households in this country are in that position.
The objection is real: this costs money the treasury has not got, and a new road is cheaper to announce and easier to photograph.

But the comparison is not between a bus service and nothing. It is between a bus service and the private arrangements families are already paying for in its absence - the school van, the hired three-wheeler to the clinic, the extra rent to live near a junction. That money is being spent. It is simply being spent by individuals, inefficiently, and it does not appear in any budget.

So the honest form of the question is not whether we can afford public transport. It is whether we would rather pay for mobility collectively and cheaply, or privately and dearly, given that we are certainly going to pay.
Put that way, the answer is not really in dispute.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: It discards the popular argument for a better one, then reframes the cost question so the conclusion follows without being asserted.

blocks.heading: 6. The Work That Is Not Counted
text: My mother rises at half past four. By the time the rest of the house is awake there is breakfast, three lunch packets, a load of washing on the line and a kitchen that has already been cleaned once. She is not employed.
That last sentence is the one I want to examine, because every form she fills describes her that way and every form is wrong.

What she does has a market price. If she stopped, the household would have to buy roughly what she supplies: cooked food, childcare for my brother, cleaning, the management of medicines for my grandmother, and the negotiation with the school, the bank and the electricity office that occupies more of her week than anybody notices. We could not afford it. That is not an opinion, it is arithmetic.
The usual response is that this work is done out of love and should not be priced. But my father's work is also done partly out of love for us, and nobody suggests that it therefore need not be paid.

The consequence of not counting it is not merely that she goes unthanked. It is that she has no pension, no leave, no bad day to which she is entitled, and no claim on anything if the marriage or her health fails. A person who works for thirty years and accumulates no security has not been honoured. She has been quietly exposed.
Calling it love does not change the arithmetic. It only makes the arithmetic harder to raise.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: One household used as the whole argument. The answer to the love objection - applying it to the father as well - is a single move that collapses the counter-case.

blocks.heading: 7. Do Examinations Measure Ability?
text: They measure a part of it, accurately, and we then use the result as though it described the whole person. The error is not in the instrument. It is in what we do with the reading.

What a three-hour paper measures well is the ability to retrieve and organise knowledge quickly, alone, under pressure, in writing. It is fashionable to dismiss this as mere memory. It is not mere anything: a great deal of serious work is done exactly under those conditions, and the anonymity of the paper means it cannot be bought, which no alternative yet proposed can claim.

What it measures badly is everything that takes longer than three hours. Patience with a problem over a month. Working with people who are difficult. Judgement where the question has not been set for you. These are not minor omissions - they are most of adult competence.

The proposed remedies mostly fail on fairness rather than on principle. Continuous assessment measures more, through a teacher who knows the family and can be leaned on. Interviews reward the confident and the coached. A crude measure that cannot be corrupted may be better than a subtle one that can.

So the reform worth arguing for is not a different examination. It is refusing to let one number stand as a verdict: universities reading more than the grades, employers looking at what a person has actually done, and adults ending the habit of asking a nineteen-year-old their results as though the answer settled the matter of who they are.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: A companion to the Grade 12 essay on the same question, written tighter and committing in the first two sentences. Comparing the two shows a class what the extra year should look like.

blocks.heading: 8. The Public Library
text: The library in our town is one room above the municipal office, and you reach it by an outside staircase with a broken third step that has been broken for as long as I have used it.

Inside there are eleven shelves. Four are Sinhala fiction, two are English, one is newspapers on a wooden rod, and the rest are reference books of an age that makes some of them historical documents rather than sources. The atlas shows countries that no longer exist.
There are two tables. From nine in the morning the same four men read the newspapers, in the same order, and there is an understanding about who has which paper that has never been written down.

The librarian is a woman of about fifty who knows what every regular reader is in the middle of. When I was in Grade 9 she put a book on the corner of the table without saying anything, because she had noticed what I had returned. She has done this perhaps twenty times and she has been wrong twice.
The building is inadequate by any standard one could write down. The ceiling leaks over the reference shelf and there is no computer.
It is also the only room in eleven kilometres where a person may sit for three hours, take nothing, buy nothing, be asked for nothing, and read.
I have thought about that sentence a good deal, and I cannot find another room it is true of.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: Description as argument. Every detail is concrete and slightly shabby, so the final claim lands as a discovery rather than a slogan.

blocks.heading: 9. A Letter to Myself at Fifteen
text: You are about to spend two years being frightened of an examination, and I cannot tell you the result, so I will tell you the four things I would have paid money to know.

First: the marks are not distributed by effort. They are distributed by effort applied to the right things, and you will spend most of Grade 10 copying notes beautifully, which feels like work and is closer to decoration. Write less and explain more, aloud, to somebody who has not read the chapter.

Second: the people who seem effortlessly clever are mostly people who started earlier or who are frightened in a quieter way than you. You will find this out in Grade 13 and it will be too late to have been comforted by it.

Third: you will lose two friendships in these two years, one by drifting and one by something you say. The second one is repairable and you will not attempt the repair for eleven months out of pride. Do it in the first week.

Fourth, and I am least sure of this: the examination matters much less than everyone around you believes and much more than the people who say so will admit. Both halves are true. Hold them together and you will neither collapse nor coast.

You will be all right. Not because of the result - I still do not know the result - but because the habit you are building of sitting down with something difficult is worth more than the paper, and nobody is going to tell you that this year.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: The letter form permits direct advice without preaching, and numbering keeps 250 words disciplined. The fourth point holds two opposing truths, which is the hardest thing in the set.

blocks.heading: 10. Reading the News in Two Languages
text: For the last two years I have read the same day's news in Sinhala and in English, partly to improve the English and partly out of curiosity. The curiosity turned out to be the more useful reason.

The facts are usually the same. What differs is what is assumed about the reader. The English report explains the background as though the reader may be unfamiliar with it and might be elsewhere. The Sinhala report assumes the reader already knows, and spends its space on what it means for us. Neither is superior. They are written for different rooms.

The difference that matters is in what gets left out. An event that is enormous in one is a paragraph in the other, and not because of any conspiracy - because each editor knows their readers and is probably right about them.

The consequence is that two people in the same town can follow the news carefully, honestly, every day, and hold pictures of the country that do not overlap. When they disagree, each assumes the other is not paying attention. Both are paying close attention to different accounts.

I do not conclude from this that everybody should read two languages; most people have neither the time nor the second language. I conclude something narrower and more troubling. The common ground we assume exists - the shared set of facts that a disagreement can be conducted across - is smaller than we think, and nobody is responsible for maintaining it.
That is not a language problem. It is what makes it hard to fix.

blocks.title: What this one shows
text: An original observation the writer could only have made by doing the thing described. It also states honestly what it does not conclude, which narrows the claim and strengthens it.

blocks.heading: How to use these with a class
bullets: **Read only the first paragraph, then stop.** Ask the class to predict the rest. If they can, the essay is properly structured; if they cannot, it is not.
**Time a full one at thirty-five minutes,** including planning and checking. That is the real constraint, and practising without it builds a habit that fails on the day.
**Mark for structure before language.** A grammatically clean essay with no argument scores below a rougher one that answers the question. Say so, or they will polish the wrong thing.
**Insist on answering the question that was set.** The commonest A/L failure is a good essay on the neighbouring topic.
**Have them cut a finished essay by fifty words.** Nothing teaches economy faster, and it shows them which sentences were carrying nothing.
